title: In the Beginning: God Makes the World
summary: God speaks the world into being over six days, bringing order out of what was formless and empty and filling it with light, sky, sea, land, plants, and living creatures. On the sixth day he makes human beings in his own image, male and female, blesses them, and gives them the earth to fill and rule. He looks at everything he has made and calls it very good.
story:
This is where the whole story starts, and it starts with God rather than with us. Before there is a people, a law, or a temple, there is a maker and a world he calls good. Everything that follows in the Bible assumes this chapter. The fall in Genesis 3 is tragic because the world was good; the rescue that runs from Abraham to Jesus is a rescue of this world, not an escape from it; and the Bible's last pages describe a new heaven and a new earth, the first creation healed and completed. When you read about exile and return, kingdom and temple, cross and resurrection, keep this chapter in mind. It is what God is getting back.

The literary unit does not end where the chapter does. The chapter division, added in the Middle Ages, stops at the sixth day, but the account runs on to the seventh day in Genesis 2:1-3, where God rests and blesses the day. Read the two together: the week is not complete, and the chapter's point is not complete, until God's rest.
historical:
Genesis doesn't tell us when it was written, and the question is debated. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses with the first five books of the Bible (the Torah, or Pentateuch), which would place their origin in the second half of the second millennium BC. Many modern scholars assign Genesis 1 to a priestly writer during or after the Babylonian exile in the sixth century BC, when Israel lived in the shadow of Babylon's temples and star-gods; others argue for older material and a much earlier core. Either way, the chapter's closest conversation partners are the creation traditions of Mesopotamia and Egypt.

The best known of those is the Babylonian epic Enuma Elish, named from its first words, ‘when on high’. Most of its tablets were copied in the first millennium BC, but W. G. Lambert dated its composition to the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I, about 1100 BC, and it was recited at Babylon's New Year festival. In its fourth tablet the god Marduk kills the sea goddess Tiamat and splits her body like a dried fish, making the sky from one half and the earth from the other; in the sixth, humanity is made from the blood of the rebel god Kingu so that people can carry the gods' labor. The older Atrahasis epic, known from copies of about the seventeenth century BC, tells the same story of human origins: clay mixed with a slain god's blood, and people made to dig the gods' canals.

Egypt offered other pictures. At Heliopolis the creator Atum rose on a mound out of the dark primeval waters called Nun. The Memphite Theology, preserved on the Shabaka Stone (a granite slab now in the British Museum, inscribed about 710 BC and claiming to copy an older text), describes the god Ptah creating through what his heart conceived and his tongue commanded, the nearest ancient analogy to creation by word, though Ptah's speech brings forth gods. The Instruction for Merikare, a Middle Kingdom wisdom text set in the late third millennium BC, says that the creator made sky and earth for humankind's sake and calls human beings his images who came from his body, a rare case of image language applied beyond the king.

When these texts were rediscovered, some scholars concluded that Genesis 1 was simply borrowed. Hermann Gunkel's Schöpfung und Chaos (1895) read it as a demythologized version of the Babylonian battle with the sea, and Friedrich Delitzsch's lectures Babel und Bibel (1902), given before Kaiser Wilhelm II, argued that the Old Testament was derivative of Babylon. Later study was more careful. Alexander Heidel (The Babylonian Genesis, 1942) set out the differences in detail; Lambert (Journal of Theological Studies, 1965) argued that Genesis shows no direct dependence on Enuma Elish; and David Tsumura (1989) argued that the Hebrew tehom, the deep, is a native Semitic word and cannot have been borrowed from the name Tiamat. The common judgment now is that Genesis 1 shares a world of images and questions with its neighbors and answers them in its own way, often with a pointed contrast.
cultural:
An ancient reader would notice at once what is missing. There is no battle. The deep and the waters, which Babylon imagined as a goddess, are simply there, without personality or resistance. The great sea creatures of verse 21 (tanninim) are the word Hebrew poetry uses for the monsters God subdues (Psalm 74:13, Isaiah 27:1, 51:9), and the Canaanite texts from Ugarit, written down around the thirteenth century BC, tell of Baal and his sister Anat defeating the sea god Yam and a many-headed serpent. Genesis 1 makes the monster a creature, created (the verb bara) and blessed. The sun and moon, worshiped across the ancient world, aren't even named; they are the greater light and the lesser light. The Hebrew shemesh, sun, is close kin to Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun god, and the moon god Sin had great temples at Ur and Harran, Abraham's cities. Babylon's scholars kept vast omen series reading the future in the stars. Genesis gives the lights a job: to shine, to separate day from night, and to mark signs, seasons (moadim, the word later used for Israel's appointed festivals in Leviticus 23), days, and years. Deuteronomy 4:16-19 later forbids images of male or female, beast, bird, creeping thing, fish, sun, moon, and stars, running back through the same list in reverse order.

The making of humanity would have startled that reader most. Kings in the ancient Near East set up statues of themselves in conquered lands as the visible sign of their rule. A statue of a ruler of Guzana found at Tell Fekheriye in Syria in 1979, inscribed in Akkadian and Aramaic in the ninth century BC, calls itself by Aramaic words cognate to both tselem, image, and demut, likeness. Egyptian kings were called the living image of a god; the name Tutankhamun means the living image of Amun. Genesis gives that title to every human being, male and female, and the humans it describes are not slaves made to relieve the gods of work, as in Atrahasis and Enuma Elish. God feeds them (verse 29) rather than being fed by them, blesses them, and gives them work: to fill the earth and rule it on his behalf. The first diet is plants for people and animals alike; permission to eat meat comes only after the flood (Genesis 9:3).

The seven-day pattern also spoke to that world. Ancient texts used a week of days as a unit of completion: in the Ugaritic Baal cycle, fire burns six days in the building of Baal's palace and on the seventh the work is finished. Temples were dedicated in sevens; Solomon's took seven years to build and was dedicated in the seventh month at a feast of seven days (1 Kings 6:38, 8:2, 8:65). Scholars such as Jon Levenson and John Walton have argued that Genesis 1 describes the world as God's temple, finished and then inhabited by God in rest on the seventh day. The Babylonian calendar marked certain days of the lunar month, and its word shapattu named the full-moon day, but no neighbor of Israel is known to have kept a continuous seven-day week independent of the moon. Israel's week and its Sabbath rest are grounded here and in Exodus 20:11.
literary:
Genesis 1 is carefully built, closer to a hymn or a liturgy than to a lab report, though it is written in prose. Each day follows a recurring pattern: an announcement (“And God said”), a command (“Let there be”), a report of fulfillment (“And it was so”), a description of the act, God's naming or blessing, an evaluation (“God saw that it was good”), and the closing formula of evening and morning with a numbered day. The pattern bends at the edges, which is part of the art. The second day has no ‘good’, perhaps because the separation of the waters is only finished on the third day, which then receives two. God names things on days one to three (day, night, sky, earth, seas) and names nothing afterward; in Genesis 2 the man names the animals.

Verse 2 names two problems, the earth “formless and void”, and the days answer them in order. Days one to three form realms (light and darkness, sky and sea, dry land with plants), and days four to six fill those same realms (lights, birds and fish, land animals and people). Day one pairs with day four, two with five, and three with six. The seventh day stands outside the pattern, with no work, no evening, and no morning.

The number seven runs through the account, as Umberto Cassuto showed in his commentary (English 1961). Verse 1 has seven Hebrew words and verse 2 has fourteen. The word God (Elohim) occurs thirty-five times in 1:1-2:3, ‘good’ seven times, and the closing paragraph on the seventh day (2:1-3) has thirty-five words. The numbered days have no definite article until the last two: literally ‘day one’, ‘a second day’, and so on, then ‘the sixth day’ and ‘the seventh day’, marking a climax. The sixth day is also the longest. The rhythm slows, God speaks in the first person plural (“Let Us make”), and verse 27 breaks into three lines of poetry, with the verb create three times: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.” The sea creatures are blessed in verse 22, but only of humanity does the text say that God spoke ‘to them’ (verse 28), and only at the end does the verdict rise from good to “very good”.

outline.t: God, the beginning, and a world formless and empty
Day two: the sky separates the waters
Day three: land, seas, and plants
Day four: sun, moon, and stars
Day five: sea creatures and birds
Day six: humanity in God's image, blessed and given work

doctrines.note: God alone creates, by his word, and the world is good because he made it. Nothing in creation is a god, and nothing in it is evil by nature: sea, monster, sun, and star are all creatures. The church later confessed this as creation from nothing, God making the world without any pre-existing stuff that rivaled him. Verse 1 does not by itself settle that doctrine (see the text note), but the whole chapter's picture of a God who meets no resistance points toward it, and later Scripture states it (Hebrews 11:3).

Every human being, male and female, bears the image of God (verses 26 and 27). The image is set in royal language: to be God's image is to represent his rule on earth, and the text joins it to blessing, fruitfulness, and dominion. Genesis 5:1-3 and 9:6 show that the image was not lost after the fall; it still grounds the value of every human life.

The first word to humanity is a blessing and a task: fill the earth, subdue it, and rule its creatures (verse 28). Work belongs to the good creation before anything goes wrong, and human rule is modeled on God's own ordering and filling of the world, not on the harsh rule the law later forbids (Leviticus 25:43).

The chapter shows who God is before it says anything about us: sovereign, orderly, generous, and delighted with what he has made. He speaks and it is done, he separates and names, he blesses and provides food. Christians have also read the Spirit of God in verse 2 and the plural of verse 26 in light of the Trinity, though many scholars think the first readers heard a plural of majesty or God addressing his heavenly court.

God does not only make the world; he orders it to continue. The lights keep days, seasons, and years, plants and animals reproduce according to their kinds, and God gives every living creature its food (verses 29 and 30). The regularities of nature are presented as God's gift and care rather than as fate or as the moods of gods.

words.note: Bara, to create. It occurs about fifty times in the Hebrew Bible, eleven of them in Genesis 1 to 6 and about twenty in Isaiah, mostly in chapters 40 to 66, where God's creating grounds the promise of a new exodus. In the forms that mean create, the verb only ever has God as its subject; people make and build, but only God creates, and the verb never names any material God works on. It appears at the three decisive points of the chapter: the heavens and the earth (verse 1), the great sea creatures and living things (verse 21), and humanity (verse 27, three times). The word itself doesn't prove creation from nothing, as the standard lexicons note, but it marks acts that belong to God alone.

Tohu, formlessness, emptiness, waste. It occurs twenty times, often of a trackless desert (Deuteronomy 32:10) or of what is futile and empty, like idols (Isaiah 44:9). Paired with bohu, void, it appears only here and in Jeremiah 4:23, where the prophet sees the land after judgment “formless and void” with no light, creation run backward. Isaiah 45:18 uses tohu to say God did not create the earth to be empty but formed it to be inhabited. Verse 2 therefore describes not evil but an unfinished world, uninhabitable and unordered, waiting for God's word.

Ruach, spirit, wind, breath. The word occurs nearly four hundred times across that full range, and English Bibles divide over verse 2: ‘the Spirit of God’ (BSB, ESV, NIV), ‘a wind from God’ (NRSV and the Jewish Publication Society's translation), or ‘a mighty wind’ taking Elohim as a superlative. Targum Onqelos reads a wind from before the LORD. The participle translated “hovering” occurs elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:11, of an eagle hovering over its young, which favors a living presence over a gust. The same Spirit gives life in Psalm 104:30 and Ezekiel 37.

Raqia, expanse, traditionally ‘firmament’ (from the Latin firmamentum, following the Greek stereoma, a solid thing). It occurs seventeen times, nine of them in this chapter; the others are in Ezekiel's visions, where it is a gleaming platform over the living creatures and beneath God's throne (Ezekiel 1:22-26, 10:1), and in Psalm 19:1, Psalm 150:1, and Daniel 12:3. The related verb means to beat out or hammer thin, used of gold and bronze plates (Exodus 39:3, Numbers 16:39). Whether the text pictures a solid dome or simply the visible sky described as it appears is debated; see the hard question.

Yom, day, one of the commonest words in the Bible (almost two thousand occurrences). Usually it means a day of daylight or a full day, but it has a range: the daylight period itself (verse 5, God called the light day), a period or time (‘in the day of trouble’), and in Genesis 2:4 the whole creation week (“in the day that the LORD God made them”). With numbers, as here, it ordinarily means an ordinary day. How to read the days is one of the chapter's great debates, set out under the hard questions.

Tselem, image. It occurs seventeen times: five in Genesis (1:26, 1:27 twice, 5:3, 9:6), and elsewhere for idols and cult statues (Numbers 33:52, 2 Kings 11:18, Ezekiel 7:20, Amos 5:26), for the golden models of tumors and rats the Philistines made (1 Samuel 6:5, 11), and in two Psalms for a shadow or phantom (39:6, 73:20). The lexicons define it as a representation, usually physical and three-dimensional. That background is the key: an image stands in a place to represent someone who rules there. Genesis 5:3 uses the same word for Seth being in Adam's image, joining the royal sense to the sense of sonship.

Demut, likeness, resemblance, a pattern. It occurs twenty-five times, sixteen of them in Ezekiel, who repeatedly describes what he saw as ‘the likeness of’ something, climaxing in the likeness of a human form on the throne of God (Ezekiel 1:26). Ahaz sends Uriah the priest a model (demut) of an altar he has seen in Damascus (2 Kings 16:10). Paired with tselem in verse 26, it probably softens and specifies the image (like, but not identical) rather than naming a second, separate gift. The distinction some church fathers drew between image and likeness rests on the Greek and Latin translations more than on the Hebrew.

Radah, to rule, have dominion. It occurs about two dozen times, used of kings (Solomon in 1 Kings 4:24, the messianic king in Psalm 72:8 and 110:2) and, tellingly, in laws forbidding Israelites to rule a fellow Israelite harshly (Leviticus 25:43, 46, 53); Ezekiel 34:4 condemns shepherds who ruled the flock with harshness. Verse 28 adds kavash, subdue, a stronger word used of bringing land under control (Numbers 32:22, Joshua 18:1) and elsewhere of forcing people into servitude (Jeremiah 34:11). In context the human task is royal stewardship on the model of God's own rule, which in this chapter orders, fills, blesses, and feeds.

christ:
The New Testament reads this chapter as the first act of a story that Christ completes. John's Gospel opens with the same words, “In the beginning”, and says that the Word who was with God and was God is the agent of this creation: “Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made” (John 1:3). Paul makes the same claim, adding that creation also has Christ as its goal: “All things were created through Him and for Him” (Colossians 1:16). Hebrews says the Son is the one “through whom He made the universe” and who goes on “upholding all things by His powerful word” (Hebrews 1:2-3). The speaking God of Genesis 1 is, for the apostles, the Father speaking through his Word.

The image of God is the chapter's richest thread. Humanity was made in God's image to represent his rule, and the New Testament calls Christ himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15) and “the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4). He is not only made in the image; he is the image, the true human who rules as a servant. Salvation is then described as restoring the image in people: believers are predestined “to be conformed to the image of His Son” (Romans 8:29), and the new self “is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (Colossians 3:10). James applies the chapter's dignity to speech: we cannot bless God and curse people “who have been made in God’s likeness” (James 3:9).

Jesus himself quotes verse 27 when asked about divorce: “from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’” (Mark 10:6), appealing to God's design over later concessions. The light that God speaks into darkness on the first day becomes Paul's picture of conversion in 2 Corinthians 4:6, where the Creator who called light out of darkness shines in human hearts in the face of Christ, and Paul can say that anyone in Christ “is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Bible ends where it began, with “a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1), and a city where “There will be no more night” because God is its light (Revelation 22:5). None of this is hidden code in Genesis 1. It is the later story showing where the first one was going.
interpretation:
Jewish readers treated this chapter with reverence and caution. The Mishnah (Hagigah 2:1) forbids expounding the work of creation (maaseh bereshit) before more than one student at a time, ranking it with the mysteries of Ezekiel's chariot vision. Philo of Alexandria, in On the Creation of the World (early first century AD), argued that the six days describe order rather than time, since God needs no time to act. The mother in 2 Maccabees 7:28 tells her son that God made heaven and earth not out of things that existed, an early statement of creation from nothing. Genesis Rabbah, the great midrash on Genesis edited in the land of Israel in the early fifth century, opens (1:1) by reading beginning through Proverbs 8:22: God looked into the Torah as an architect consults a plan and created the world. On verse 26 it imagines the angels divided over whether humanity should be made, with Truth and Peace objecting, and God casting Truth to the earth (8:5). Rashi (eleventh century) begins his commentary by asking why the Torah starts with creation rather than the first commandment of Exodus 12, and answers with Rabbi Isaac that the Creator owns the earth and may give the land to whom he wills; he also read verse 1 as a dependent clause, as noted under the text.

Christian readers began early. Theophilus of Antioch (To Autolycus 2.15, about AD 180) took the three days before the lights as types of God, his Word, and his Wisdom, the first surviving use of the Greek word for Trinity. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.6.1) distinguished the image, which all people bear, from the likeness, received through the Spirit. Origen (On First Principles, book 4) asked how there could be a first, second, and third day with evening and morning before the sun, and read the days figuratively. Basil of Caesarea preached nine homilies on the six days in Lent of 378, marveling at the natural world, and Ambrose followed him in Latin. Augustine returned to the chapter again and again, in the last three books of the Confessions and in The Literal Meaning of Genesis (401 to 415), where he argued that God created all things at once and that the days describe an order of angelic knowledge. Ephrem the Syrian, by contrast, insisted on ordinary days. Thomas Aquinas treated the work of the six days in Summa Theologiae I, questions 65 to 74, weighing Augustine against the literal reading. Luther's lectures on Genesis (1535 to 1545) defended six ordinary days, while Calvin's commentary (1554) argued that Moses accommodated his language to ordinary people, noting that astronomers had shown Saturn to be larger than the moon.

Modern readers have divided along new lines. Gunkel (1895) placed the chapter in the history of ancient myth; Karl Barth's Church Dogmatics III/1 (1945) read creation as the external basis of the covenant and found the image in the relation of male and female; Gerhard von Rad and Claus Westermann read it as priestly confession. J. Richard Middleton (The Liberating Image, 2005) developed the royal reading of the image, and Jon Levenson (Creation and the Persistence of Evil, 1988), a Jewish scholar, argued that the chapter contains chaos rather than abolishing it.

The chapter has a long life in worship. In the synagogue it is read on Simchat Torah, immediately after the last verses of Deuteronomy, so that the Torah's end runs straight into its beginning, and again on the following Sabbath. In the church it is the first reading of the Easter Vigil, and the Revised Common Lectionary appoints it for Trinity Sunday in Year A. Michelangelo painted the separation of light from darkness, the creation of sun and moon, and the creation of Adam on the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512). Haydn's oratorio The Creation (first performed in Vienna in 1798) sets the creation of light with a sudden fortissimo chord that stunned its first audiences. On Christmas Eve 1968 the crew of Apollo 8, orbiting the moon, read verses 1 to 10 from the King James Version to a worldwide television audience.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter, mostly over grammar rather than manuscripts.

Verse 1 can be read as an independent sentence or as a dependent clause. Most translations (and the Greek Septuagint, the Latin Vulgate, and the Masoretic accents, which mark a pause after the first word) read ‘In the beginning God created’, a heading or first act. Rashi and Ibn Ezra, noting that bereshit normally stands before another noun, read ‘When God began to create’, and the Jewish Publication Society's translation of 1985 follows them, as does the NRSV (1989) with ‘In the beginning when God created’. On the second reading verse 2 describes the condition that already existed when God began, and the verse does not by itself state creation from nothing; on the first, verse 1 describes the absolute beginning. Both are grammatically possible, and scholars remain divided.

In verse 2 the choice between ‘Spirit’ and ‘wind’ is interpretive, as explained under the word ruach. In verse 26 the standard Hebrew reads ‘over all the earth’ in a list of animals; the Syriac version reads ‘over all the wild animals of the earth’, which matches the list better and which the NRSV adopts.

The Septuagint has two additions. After verse 8 it includes ‘and God saw that it was good’ for the second day, and after verse 9 it reports that the water was gathered and the dry land appeared, completing the pattern of command and fulfillment. Both are usually judged to be smoothings, since a scribe is more likely to complete a pattern than to break one. The Septuagint also translates image and likeness as eikōn and homoiōsis, and the Latin as imago and similitudo, which gave later theology its vocabulary.

The verse numbers are the same in Hebrew and English Bibles here. The chapter break, however, came much later than the text; the chapter divisions now used were added in the Middle Ages (commonly attributed to Stephen Langton, early thirteenth century), and this one separates the six days from the seventh.

teach.big: The one true God made everything by his word, ordered it, filled it, called it very good, and made every human being in his image to represent his rule with care.

outline.t: Everything that exists begins with God, and the world starts unformed and unfilled but already under the hovering presence of his Spirit.
God's first act is light: he speaks, sees that it is good, separates, and names, the pattern of all his work.
God sets bounds to the waters that other peoples feared; what they worshiped or dreaded is simply ordered by his word.
Dry land and plants appear, and the earth itself is given power to produce life according to God's design.
The sun, moon, and stars that nations worshiped are unnamed lamps, set to serve by marking time; creation keeps time for worship.
God fills sea and sky and blesses even the great sea creatures; nothing in the world is a rival god.
The land is filled with animals of every kind, and each is good in God's eyes before humanity arrives.
Humanity, male and female, is made in God's image, blessed, and commissioned to fill the earth and rule it as God's representatives.
God provides food for every creature, and the whole creation, with humanity in it, is very good.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misuse turns the chapter into a battlefield between science and faith, as though its main point were the age of the earth. Faithful Christians hold several readings of the days (see the hard questions), and a teacher who makes one of them the test of faith has added to the text. The opposite mistake treats the chapter as mere myth with nothing to say about the real world. It makes real claims: one God, a good creation, and human beings made in his image.

A second misuse reads dominion as license. The chapter's model for human rule is God's own rule, which orders, blesses, and feeds, and Israel's law forbids ruling another person harshly. A third reduces the image of God to one faculty, such as reason, which quietly suggests that people with less capacity bear less of it. The text ties the image to the whole human creature, male and female, and to a calling. A fourth presses verse 26 as a proof of the Trinity, which overstates what the first readers could have heard; it is better to say that the chapter's Spirit and speaking God find their full meaning in the New Testament. Finally, don't use “Be fruitful and multiply” to shame people who are single or childless. It is a blessing on the race, not a command that condemns those who never marry or cannot have children, and the New Testament honors both.
teach.pastoral: This chapter tells every person in the room that they bear God's image, and it will land hard on some. People who have been told they are worthless, abused, disabled, or discarded need to hear that their dignity comes from God's decision, not from their usefulness. Teach it so that it lifts them rather than simply informing the strong. Be gentle with those who long for children and cannot have them; the blessing of fruitfulness can sound like a verdict on their bodies. And be patient with those who struggle with the science questions: give them the range of faithful readings rather than an ultimatum.

hard.q: Are these six literal days, and can Genesis 1 be squared with modern science?
hard.a:
The objection comes from two directions. Critical scholars and many skeptics argue that the chapter plainly teaches an ancient cosmology: a solid dome (raqia) holding back waters above the sky, light before the sun, plants before the sun, and a complete world in six days, all of which modern science contradicts. Paul Seely, writing as an evangelical in the Westminster Theological Journal (1991), argued that the raqia really was understood as a solid dome, as nearly every ancient people believed, and that God accommodated revelation to that view. From the other side, young-earth creationists such as John Whitcomb and Henry Morris (The Genesis Flood, 1961) argue that the plain sense is six ordinary days a few thousand years ago and that any other reading bends Scripture to fit science; Luther, in his lectures on Genesis, also insisted on ordinary days.

Christians who share the same confession about God as creator answer in several ways. The young-earth reading keeps the days as ordinary days and challenges the science. The day-age view, defended for example by Hugh Ross (A Matter of Days, 2004), takes each day as a long age. The framework view, proposed by Arie Noordtzij in 1924 and developed by Meredith Kline and Henri Blocher (In the Beginning, 1984), argues from the matching of days one to three with four to six that the week is a literary frame arranging God's works topically. C. John Collins (Genesis 1-4, 2006) reads the days as analogical, God's workweek as the pattern for ours. John Walton (The Lost World of Genesis One, 2009) reads the chapter as God inaugurating the cosmos as his temple, assigning functions rather than describing material origins. Calvin's principle of accommodation, that Moses described the heavens as they appear, is invoked by several of these views. The question is also older than modern science: Origen and Augustine both doubted that the days were ordinary days, while Basil and Ephrem took them as ordinary.

What the chapter plainly teaches, on every one of these readings, is who made the world, what it is for, and who we are in it. That is the church's first-order confession. How long it took and how its picture of the sky relates to modern cosmology are second-order questions on which faithful readers differ.

hard.q: Isn't Genesis 1 just a Hebrew version of Babylonian myth?
hard.a:
The case for dependence is serious. Both Genesis 1 and Enuma Elish begin with waters, divide them to make sky and earth, speak of a deep (tehom and Tiamat sound alike), set the heavenly bodies to mark time, and end with the creation of humanity and a resting deity. Hermann Gunkel (1895) argued that Genesis 1 was a demythologized form of the Babylonian combat with the sea, and Friedrich Delitzsch (1902) drew the conclusion that the Bible was derivative and not revelation. Many critical scholars still hold that Israel's priests wrote the chapter in Babylonian exile as a reply to Babylon's myth. The Jewish scholar Jon Levenson (1988) adds that elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible God does fight the sea and its monsters (Psalm 74:13-14, Isaiah 51:9), so that the combat myth survives inside Israel's own faith.

The responses are also serious. Alexander Heidel (The Babylonian Genesis, 1942) set out the differences, which are larger than the likenesses: no theogony (birth of gods), no battle, no divine body split in two, no humans made from divine blood to serve as laborers. W. G. Lambert, one of the leading Assyriologists of his generation, concluded (1965) that Genesis shows no direct dependence on Enuma Elish, and David Tsumura (1989, and Creation and Destruction, 2005) argued that tehom is a common Semitic word that cannot derive from the name Tiamat. Many scholars, including Nahum Sarna in his JPS commentary (1989), read the likenesses as signs of a shared world and the differences as deliberate: Genesis speaks in the vocabulary of its neighbors in order to deny what they believed. Whether that polemic is aimed at Babylon in the exile or at the whole ancient world earlier is part of the dating debate. On any view, borrowing a picture is not the same as borrowing a theology, and the theology of Genesis 1 has no ancient parallel.

observe: Trace the repeated phrases through the six days. Where does the pattern change, and what is different about the sixth and seventh days?
Which things does God name, which does he bless, and which does he call good? What does he say to humanity that he says to no other creature?
Compare days one to three with days four to six. How do they match?
interpret: Why might Genesis call the sun and moon the greater light and the lesser light instead of using their names?
What does it mean that humanity is made in God's image, in light of how ancient kings used images of themselves?
How should God's own way of ruling in this chapter shape what dominion over the earth means for us?
apply: What does it change about how you see a stranger, an enemy, or yourself to believe that every person bears the image of God?
The chapter calls the physical world good, and very good. Where do you tend to treat the body, work, or the created world as less spiritual than it is?
Neighboring peoples feared the sea and worshiped the sun. What powers do people fear or trust today that Genesis 1 would call mere creatures?
